pages.text: Lungs and Breathing

image.note: Cover: a child breathing in, lungs glowing in the chest

pages.text: Contents. Why We Breathe / Inside Your Lungs / In and Out / The Amazing Breath / Looking After Your Lungs / The Breath of Life.

Take a deep breath. Now let it out. You just did something you will do more than twenty thousand times today, and almost never think about once. Breathing is so automatic that you forget it entirely, and yet without it you would last only minutes. This is the story of the quiet machine that keeps you alive: your lungs.

image.note: A child taking a deep breath, lungs glowing

pages.text: You are breathing right now, as you read this, in and out, in and out, and you did not decide to. Your body does it for you, awake or asleep. But what exactly happens, each time the air goes in? Why must it? Where does it go? Let us follow a single breath, all the way down.

image.note: A cutaway of the chest, the air path highlighted

pages.text: Everything alive needs energy, and to make energy from your food, your body needs one thing above all: oxygen, a gas in the air all around you. Air is not empty. It is full of tiny gases, and about one part in five is the oxygen your body cannot live without.

image.note: Air made of tiny gas particles, oxygen highlighted

pages.text: Every tiny part of you, every muscle, every thought in your brain, is powered by oxygen, burning your food like a fire needs air to burn. And like any fire, this makes a waste gas: carbon dioxide, which the body must get rid of. So breathing does two jobs at once: it brings the good gas in, and sends the waste gas out.

image.note: Oxygen in, carbon dioxide out, at a body cell

pages.text: That is why you cannot hold your breath for long. Try it, and soon your body forces you to gasp. It is not really the lack of oxygen you feel first, but the build-up of waste carbon dioxide, your body shouting that it must breathe out, now. Your breath, it turns out, is not really yours to hold.

image.note: A child holding their breath, then gasping

pages.text: So where does the air go? Down a tube in your throat called the windpipe, held always open by rings of gristle so it never collapses, like the ridged hose of a vacuum cleaner. Put your fingers on the front of your neck, and you can feel it.

image.note: The windpipe with its rings of cartilage

pages.text: At the bottom, the windpipe splits in two, one branch into each lung, and then splits again, and again, and again, into thousands of ever-smaller tubes, like the branches of an upside-down tree growing inside your chest. This is why lungs are sometimes drawn as two great pink trees.

image.note: The branching airways like an upside-down tree

pages.text: At the tips of the smallest branches sit tiny air sacs, too small to see, called alveoli. You have hundreds of millions of them, and if you could unfold them all and lay them flat, they would cover half a tennis court. All that, folded away inside your chest.

image.note: Clusters of tiny alveoli air sacs

pages.text: These air sacs are where the magic happens. Each one is wrapped in the thinnest blood vessels, and through their walls, thinner than paper, the oxygen slips out of the air and into your blood, while the waste carbon dioxide slips the other way, out of your blood and into the air, ready to be breathed away.

image.note: Oxygen and carbon dioxide swapping at an air sac

pages.text: But how does the air get in and out? Your lungs cannot pull or push, for they are not muscles. The real work is done below them, by a great sheet of muscle stretched across your body under the lungs, called the diaphragm.

image.note: The dome-shaped diaphragm below the lungs

pages.text: When the diaphragm pulls down and flattens, it makes more room in your chest, and air rushes in to fill it. When it relaxes and domes up again, it squeezes the air back out. Down, in. Up, out. It is doing it right now, this very second, and it has never once stopped since the day you were born.

image.note: Diaphragm flattening for in, doming for out

pages.text: Put a hand on your belly and breathe deeply, and you can feel it: the gentle rise and fall as the diaphragm works below. Singers, swimmers, and players of wind instruments learn to master this muscle, but it will keep working perfectly well whether you think about it or not.

image.note: A hand on the belly, feeling the breath

pages.text: Your breathing changes to match what you do, all by itself. Sit still, and it is slow and quiet. Run a race, and your muscles roar for oxygen, and your breathing races too, deep and fast, to feed them. You do not command it. Your clever body reads your needs and answers them.

image.note: Resting breath beside racing breath

pages.text: Breathing does more than keep you alive. It lets you speak, and sing, and shout, and laugh, for your voice is made by air pushed up from the lungs, past two small flaps in your throat that flutter and make sound. Every word you have ever said, you said on a breath.

image.note: Air passing the voice box to make sound

pages.text: It lets you smell, too, for scents ride into your nose on the air you breathe. And a sudden breath can protect you: a cough is a violent breath out, blasting away anything that should not be in your airways, and a sneeze can rush out faster than a car on a motorway. Your breath is a bodyguard as well as a fuel line.

image.note: A cough clearing the airway

pages.text: Your lungs work hard for you, and they must last a lifetime, so it is worth keeping them well. The best gift you can give them is exercise: running, playing, swimming. When you make your lungs work, you make them stronger and roomier, better at their job, just as exercise strengthens any part of you.

image.note: Children running and playing, lungs working well

pages.text: Fresh, clean air is best for lungs. Smoke of any kind is their enemy, for it coats and clogs those delicate air sacs and stops them working. This is why smoking is so harmful, and why clean air matters so much for everyone. Your lungs love nothing better than a deep breath of fresh, clean air.

image.note: Fresh clean air beside smoky air

pages.text: Sometimes lungs struggle, as with the tight chest of asthma, which many people have and manage well with a doctor's help. But for most of us, most of the time, our lungs simply do their quiet work, breath after breath, and ask nothing in return but a little fresh air and a good run about.

image.note: A child using an inhaler calmly, others playing

pages.text: So the next time you take a deep breath, think of the journey it makes: down the windpipe, through the branching tree, into a hundred million tiny sacs, and out into your blood to feed every corner of you, while the waste rushes back the other way and out into the air. All that, in one quiet breath.

image.note: The full journey of one breath traced through the body

pages.text: You will breathe about twenty thousand times before you sleep tonight, and twenty thousand more tomorrow, and you will notice almost none of them. That is the wonder of your lungs: they do one of the most important jobs in your body, over and over, for your whole life, and never ask you to remember.

image.note: A child asleep, breathing peacefully

pages.text: Words to know. Oxygen: the gas your body needs from the air. Carbon dioxide: the waste gas you breathe out. Windpipe: the tube carrying air to the lungs. Alveoli: the tiny air sacs where gases swap. Diaphragm: the muscle that pulls air in and pushes it out.

image.note: Labelled diagram of the breathing system

pages.text: Your lungs feed every part of you with oxygen. But the oxygen must travel, carried by your blood, pumped by your heart, to reach every corner. Lungs and heart, breath and blood, working together this very second. Which part of your amazing body will you explore next?

image.note: Lungs and heart working together
